meta.title: Who really said "Let Us Hope Darwinism is Not True, But If It is, Let Us Pray It Does Not Become Widely Known"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Darwin. The line is an unsourced Victorian anecdote, earliest documented in R. F. Horton’s 1893 Yale lectures — and worded differently there.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Let Us Hope Darwinism is Not True, But If It is, Let Us Pray It Does Not Become Widely Known'?
meta.ogDescription: Darwin never said it. Quote Investigator calls it apocryphal; the earliest version is an unnamed “spinster” in an 1893 book of Yale lectures on preaching.

answer.label: Not Charles Darwin — a Victorian anecdote told about him
answer.sourceLine: Darwin never wrote or said this — the line is a reaction against his theory, put in the mouth of an unnamed listener. The earliest appearance known to Quote Investigator ↗ is in the English preacher R. F. Horton’s 1893 Yale lectures, where “a timid and decorous spinster” says something rather different: “Let us hope it is not true, or if it is, let us hush it up.” The familiar “let us pray it does not become widely known” wording, and every named speaker attached to it since, arrived decades later.

source.heading: Where the trail actually starts

docMeta.dd: Verbum Dei: The Yale Lectures on Preaching, 1893
Robert F. Horton (1855–1934), English Congregational minister

“a timid and decorous spinster” — unnamed, undated, never identified

source.excerpt: The Church swarms with people who have no spiritual sinew, and whose lungs cannot breathe the invigorating air of Truth: they take up the cry of that timid and decorous spinster who, on hearing an exposition of the Darwinian theory that men are descended from apes, said, “Let us hope it is not true, or if it is, let us hush it up.”
trail: 1893 — The earliest version known to Quote Investigator appears in R. F. Horton’s Yale lectures, published as Verbum Dei. A “timid and decorous spinster” says, “Let us hope it is not true, or if it is, let us hush it up.” Confirmed on page 132 of the scanned first edition ↗.

1924 — The wording most people know today surfaces. QI records Hugh Crichton-Miller’s The New Psychology and the Preacher giving an “old lady” the line “let us pray that it may not become widely known” ↗.

1941 — A named person is attached for the first time: per QI, M. F. Ashley Montagu writes in The Journal of Heredity of “the wife of the Canon of Worcester Cathedral.” That citation is QI’s. Montagu told the story again in his 1942 book Man’s Most Dangerous Myth, where, as Riley Black notes for National Geographic, he supplied no reference ↗.
1977 — Leakey and Lewin’s Origins promotes her to the Bishop of Worcester’s wife and fixes the scene in June 1860 — a date and a speaker that appear in no earlier telling QI could find ↗.
source.excerptNote: Read in the scanned Macmillan first edition. Note what is not here: no bishop, no wife, no Oxford, no 1860 — and not the famous “let us pray it does not become widely known” wording. Horton is using the line as a jab at preachers who avoid uncomfortable scholarship, not reporting an event.

artifact.linkText: Read Verbum Dei (1893) at the Internet Archive

source.useLine: Free to use in the US — but only the 1893 Horton sentence, “Let us hope it is not true, or if it is, let us hush it up,” which was published well before the 1931 cutoff and needs no permission. The familiar modern wording, “let us pray it does not become widely known,” is an anonymous later mutation with no identifiable author or fixed source, so no rights status can be asserted for it. Quote the 1893 sentence if you need cleared text — and do not credit either form to Darwin.
source.rightsNote: The passage quoted above is from Verbum Dei: The Yale Lectures on Preaching, 1893, published by Macmillan & Co. in New York and London in 1893 — comfortably before 1931, and therefore public domain in the United States. One honest caveat: the popular modern wording (“let us pray it does not become widely known”) is not Horton’s. It is an anonymous later mutation of the anecdote with no identifiable author or fixed source, so no rights status can be asserted for that form of the sentence.

author.name: Robert Forman Horton
author.heading: So who actually told this story?
author.metaLine: 1855–1934 · English Congregational minister · Yale Lyman Beecher lecturer, 1893
author.bio: Horton was an English Congregational minister who served Lyndhurst Road Congregational Church in Hampstead for fifty years, and who delivered the Lyman Beecher lectures at Yale in 1893 ↗. Those lectures were published the same year as Verbum Dei, and on page 132 he reaches for a one-line joke about people who would rather not know an uncomfortable truth. He gives the speaker no name, no date and no place — which is exactly why Quote Investigator suggests he may have invented her as a rhetorical device rather than reported her. Everything the quote later became grew out of that unsourced aside.

copyAttribution: Apocryphal — not Charles Darwin. The earliest documented form is "Let us hope it is not true, or if it is, let us hush it up," spoken by an unnamed "timid and decorous spinster" in Robert F. Horton, Verbum Dei: The Yale Lectures on Preaching, 1893 (New York and London: Macmillan & Co., 1893), page 132. The familiar "let us pray it does not become widely known" wording, and the "Bishop of Worcester's wife" attribution, are later additions with no primary source. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Everyone this has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is not a quote with one misattribution — it is a quote with a century of them. Because the speaker was anonymous from the very first telling, each retelling was free to supply a name, and each new name was repeated as fact. Searchers often arrive asking whether Darwin himself said it — he did not, and no specialist source records the line as a Darwin attribution: it is an objection to his work, not a statement of it.

items.why: The remark is a reaction to hearing Darwin’s theory expounded, not a statement of it. In the 1893 text ↗ the speaker is a listener recoiling from “the Darwinian theory that men are descended from apes.” Even Wikiquote’s list of Darwin misattributions ↗ does not include it.

items.who: The wife of the Bishop of Worcester
items.why: Quote Investigator records this version entering print in Richard Leakey and Roger Lewin’s Origins (1977), which dates the remark to June 1860. The anecdote itself is first documented in 1893 with no named speaker, no date and no place ↗.

items.who: The wife of a Canon of Worcester Cathedral
items.why: Per QI, the first identifiable person attached to the story appears in M. F. Ashley Montagu’s August 1941 piece in The Journal of Heredity — that citation is QI’s. Montagu repeated the anecdote in his 1942 book Man’s Most Dangerous Myth, and, writing for National Geographic, Riley Black notes that he gave no reference for it ↗.

QI records this attribution in The Altruistic Species (2007). It also collides with the Worcester versions: Wilberforce was Bishop of Oxford, and it was Huxley he sparred with at the 1860 Oxford meeting ↗.

QI notes that Nicholas Humphrey’s Leaps of Faith (1996) names this speaker and relocates the episode to the 1880s rather than 1860 ↗ — a different diocese and a different decade from the Worcester tellings.

misattribution.truthLine: No one has produced a Victorian source for any of it. Quote Investigator found no trace of the remark in the 1860s, 1870s or 1880s ↗ and judges it apocryphal; the trail begins with an unnamed woman in a preacher’s 1893 lecture, and every name added since was added by someone who was not there.

context.heading: Why this one keeps travelling
lead: It is a perfect story, which is the problem. A comfortable Victorian lady hears that human beings descend from apes and, rather than argue, simply hopes the news can be suppressed — a whole worldview collapsing into one line of polite panic. Anecdotes that good rarely need a source to survive.

What the record actually shows is a joke slowly acquiring a cast. In 1893 the speaker is a nameless “timid and decorous spinster” in a preacher’s lecture about intellectual cowardice in the pulpit. Over the following century, as Quote Investigator documents ↗, she becomes a society lady, an old woman, a canon’s wife, a bishop’s wife, and finally a specific bishop’s wife at a specific 1860 debate — gaining precision at every retelling while never gaining a citation.
detailsBody: The two halves of the quote have different histories. Horton’s 1893 punchline is “let us hush it up” — blunt, and about censorship. Quote Investigator records the modern “let us pray that it may not become widely known” phrasing appearing in Hugh Crichton-Miller’s The New Psychology and the Preacher in 1924, attributed to an “old lady.”

Names arrive later still. QI notes that the first identifiable attribution comes in an August 1941 article by M. F. Ashley Montagu in The Journal of Heredity, naming “the wife of the Canon of Worcester Cathedral.” Writing for National Geographic, Riley Black (published in 2009 under her former byline, Brian Switek) independently traced the story’s popular takeoff to Montagu, pointing to his 1942 book Man’s Most Dangerous Myth and noting that Montagu supplied no reference at all ↗.

The promotion from canon’s wife to bishop’s wife happens in 1977, when Richard Leakey and Roger Lewin’s Origins assigns it to the wife of the Bishop of Worcester and dates it to June 1860 — more than eight decades after Horton first told it without a date at all.
context.pull: The anecdote got more specific the further it travelled from anything anyone had witnessed.

schema.verdictNote: Apocryphal — not Charles Darwin, who is never recorded as the speaker in any telling. The earliest documented appearance is R. F. Horton’s Verbum Dei (1893), where the line is given to an unnamed “timid and decorous spinster”; Quote Investigator treats her as a rhetorical archetype rather than a real person, so Horton is the earliest documented teller, not an established author of the saying.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the anecdote is apocryphal, found no evidence in the 1860s/1870s/1880s, gives 1893 Horton's Verbum Dei as the earliest citation with a 'timid and decorous spinster', records the 'let us pray that it may not become widely known' wording in Crichton-Miller 1924, Montagu's Aug 1941 Journal of Heredity as the first identifiable attribution ('wife of the Canon of Worcester Cathedral'), Leakey & Lewin's Origins 1977 for 'wife of the Bishop of Worcester' dated June 1860, Humphrey's Leaps of Faith 1996 for the Bishop of Birmingham's wife in the 1880s, and Flescher & Worthen 2007 for Samuel Wilberforce's wife.

Page 132 of the 1893 Macmillan edition of Verbum Dei contains the sentence: 'they take up the cry of that timid and decorous spinster who, on hearing an exposition of the Darwinian theory that men are descended from apes, said, "Let us hope it is not true, or if it is, let us hush it up."' The item is Verbum Dei. The Yale lectures on preaching, 1893, by Robert F. Horton (1855-1934), Macmillan & Co., New York and London, 1893.

Riley Black's National Geographic article (bylined Riley Black; published 11 August 2009, when the author wrote as Brian Switek) traces the quote's popular takeoff to Ashley Montagu (Man's Most Dangerous Myth, 1942), states Montagu provided no reference, notes attributions have shifted among the Bishop of Worcester's wife, the Bishop of Exeter's wife and unnamed Victorian women with no original source ever provided, and characterises the story as suspicious and possibly apocryphal.

The 1860 Oxford evolution debate took place at the Oxford University Museum, with the main discussion on 30 June 1860; Samuel Wilberforce was Bishop of Oxford and his principal opponent was Thomas Henry Huxley; no remark of the form 'let us hope it is not true' is recorded, and the Bishop of Worcester is not mentioned.

Robert Forman Horton (1855-1934) was an English Congregationalist minister at Lyndhurst Road Congregational Church, Hampstead, for fifty years, and delivered the Lyman Beecher lectures at Yale in 1893, published as Verbum Dei: The Yale Lectures on Preaching (Macmillan & Co, New York, 1893).

Wikiquote's Charles Darwin page has a Misattributed section (Megginson, Ritchie R. Ward, Lord Bowen, the two Lady Hope fabrications, and the Thomas Dixon passage) and does NOT contain the 'let us hope it is not true' / 'hush it up' / 'become widely known' quote anywhere on the page.
